# Equivalent methods

The SML allows member states to use non-reference methods if it can be verified that it provides equivalent results as the reference method.

<br>

## Equivalence by law

The SML mentions that the currently listed reference methods - which are all ISO-standards - will be considered equivalent to CEN methods which will then play the role of reference methods.
This is method equivalence by law.

<!-- equivalence by law without statistical validation? -->

<br>

## Statistical testing of equivalence

For the statistical examination of methodological equivalence of two methods, we recommend doing a Bland-Altman analysis together with a ROPE-test (ROPE = region of practical equivalence).

The Bland-Altman procedure plots the difference of two methods ($D = Y - X$) against the average of both methods ($M = \frac{Y + X}{2}$).
When the soil descriptor is right-skewed, often the relative difference is used instead of the absolute difference ($D = \frac{Y - X}{M}$).
The Bland-Altman procedure defines the bias of the non-reference method versus the reference method as the average of the differences and defines the limits of agreement between both methods as the $(\frac{\alpha}{2}; 1 - \frac{\alpha}{2})$ quantiles of the differences:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{bias} &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^ND_i \\
P(D_i \in \text{LoA}) &= 1 - \alpha
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-BlandAltman} 

This is a good first visual tool when examining equivalence of two methods.
It is important to verify in a Bland-Altman analysis whether the variability of the differences is approximately equal across the range of the soil descriptor; when this is not the case a relative difference is recommended.
In @fig-blandaltman we show an example with simulated data, mimicking a soil descriptor like pH.

```{r}
#| label: fig-blandaltman
#| fig-cap: "Example of a Bland-Altman analysis."

library(tidyverse)
library(bayestestR)

# simulate data ~ soil pH
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(100, mean = 7, sd = 2)
y <- rnorm(100, mean = x, sd = .1)
df <- data.frame(
  x = x, 
  y = y,
  d = y - x,
  m = (x + y) / 2
)

# Bland-Altman plot
bias <- mean(df$d)
loa  <- quantile(df$d, c(.025, .975))

ggplot(df, aes(m, d)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "blue", fill = "blue", alpha = .1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = bias, lty = 3, color = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = bias - .02, label = "bias", color = "blue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = loa, lty = 3, color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = loa - .02, label = "LoA", color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(3, 10, 1)) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(x = "M = (Y + X) / 2",
       y = "D = Y - X",
       caption = "simulated data")
```

Statistical testing of the equivalence of two methods can be done formally with a ROPE-test. 
This procedure requires specification by the researcher of an interval $\left[\delta_l, \delta_u\right]$ (most often symmetric around zero, but could be asymmetric) that represents a region of practical equivalence (ROPE). 
All values within this range can be considered to be practically equivalent to each other
When the 95% highest density interval of the differences $D_i$ falls completely inside the ROPE, then the two methods can be considered equivalent to each other with 95% probability.
This method requires a-priori agreement among soil scientists which values of $\delta$ to be used for each soil descriptor (and choice of absolute or relative scale).
In @fig-rope we show an example, with the same data as the Bland-Altman example, of the ROPE test using $\delta = \pm 0.15$ (arbitrary value).

```{r}
#| label: fig-rope
#| fig-cap: "Example of a ROPE test"

delta <- c(-0.15, 0.15)

rope_d <- rope(df$d, range = delta)
plot(rope_d) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.1, y = 1, label = "ROPE") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  geom_rug(data = df, inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(x = d)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "D = Y - X", y = "", title = "",
       caption = "simulated data")
```

A large proportion of the differences fall within the ROPE, but the 95% HDI is not completely inside the ROPE, giving an undecided conclusion: these methods would not be considered equivalent.

```{r}
equivalence_test(df$d, ci_method = "HDI", ci = .95, range = delta)
```

<br>

## Equivalence based on ringtest reproducibility

When expert agreement on thresholds for equivalence cannot be obtained, a statistical method to derive thresholds can be based on so-called inter-laboratory ringtests. 
Ringtests are described in an ISO-standard @iso57252025 and can be used to derive a measure of reproducibility of a certain lab method.
Reproducibility is composed of within-lab variability (repeatability) and between-lab variability.
In statistical notation, the variance can be written as the sum of the variance of both components:

$$
\sigma^2_R = \sigma^2_{\text{reproducibility}} = \sigma^2_{\text{repeatability}} + \sigma^2_{\text{inter-laboratory}}
$${#eq-ringtest}

Reproducibility of the SML reference methods for a soil descriptor can be measured through such a ringtest.
The thresholds to define equivalence of a non-reference method can then be based on the level of reproducibility of the reference method.
If the reference method $Y$ is reproducible up to a value of $\sigma^2_R$, then a non-reference method $X$ could be defined as equivalent if the difference has an expected value of 0 over the whole range of the soil descriptor and if the difference falls within a pre-defined range with a certain probability (for example a range of 2 times $\sigma^2_R$ with a probability of 95%):

$$
\begin{aligned}
D &= Y - X \\
E[D|X] &= 0 \\
P(D \in \pm k \sigma_R) &= 1 - \alpha
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-equivalence}

Ringtests that examine multiple samples spread over a large range of the soil descriptor allow to calculate the reproducibility in function of the value of the soil descriptor: $\sigma_R(Y)$.
Soil descriptors can have different levels of reproducibility for small or large values; often the reproducibility variance increases for larger values of the soil descriptor.

Below we show a worked example of how this procedure can be performed.
... include a worked example of the procedure ...

```{r}
#| label: fig-ringtest
#| fig-caption: "Data from an inter-laboratory ringtest"

library(ringtest)
data("ringtest_demo")

cellstats <- calc_cell_stats(ringtest_demo) |> 
  calc_mandel_hk()

outliers <- test_outliers(cellstats)

ringtest_demo_clean <- ringtest_demo |> 
  filter(
    !(lab == "Lab_08" & level == "Level_2"),
    !(lab == "Lab_10" & level == "Level_5")
  )

ggplot(ringtest_demo_clean, aes(level, value, color = lab)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge()) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Sample Id", y = "soil descriptor (A.U.)", 
       caption = "simulated data", color = "Lab code")
```

```{r}

precision_tbl <- precision(ringtest_demo_clean)

fit2 <- with(precision_tbl, fit_precision_relationship(m_hat, s_R, rel = "II"))

ggplot(precision_tbl, aes(m_hat, s_R)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit2$fitted, color = fit2$rel)) +
  labs(title = "Reproducibility", color = "Type of relationship (ISO)")

set.seed(123)
N <- 100
y <- runif(N, 10, 50)
s <- fit2$params[1] + fit2$params[2] * y
x <- rnorm(N, mean = y, sd = s)

df <- data.frame(y = y, x = x, s = s)

ggplot(df, aes(y, y - x)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  geom_line(aes(y = 2*s), lty = 2, color = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = -2*s), lty = 2, color = "blue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2, color = "blue") +
  labs(x = "reference method", y = "diff(reference - new) method")
```
